Hi Jane —

Attached is a compact sample invoice (redwood_sample_invoice_v1.csv) plus a short explanation below. I copied the team for any additional detail. High level:

- Context banding: We bucket tokens by defined bands (0-8k, 8k-32k, 32k+). Billing applies per-token rate for each band. When a single generated response crosses a band boundary we prorate tokens to the corresponding band rates for that request.
- Rounding/minimums: We round aggregated monthly token usage per customer to the nearest 1,000 tokens (down for under-threshold customers, up when over). There is a hard monthly minimum of 10,000 tokens for pay-as-you-go accounts; enterprise pilots can request temporary waivers.
- Pilot concession: We can offer a time-boxed smoothing credit — e.g., first 30 days we apply a 50% credit on tokens billed above the 32k threshold up to a cap. This is a negotiable concession and recorded as a credit line item on invoices.

Quick sample (see attached CSV for line items):
- Call A: 28,500 request+response tokens -> billed at 8k band + remainder at 8k-32k band (no long-context premium).
- Call B: 34,200 tokens -> 32k band rates applied to first 32k, remaining 2,200 billed at 32k+ premium.
- Monthly aggregation: sum all per-call bucketed tokens, then apply rounding to nearest 1,000 tokens and attach credits if in pilot.

If you want, Kimberly can outline standard concession language we use in pilots so legal sees the exact clause.

Best,
Naomi Feldman

Hi Jane, Naomi — quick note from sales/legal side with concrete language we typically propose.

1) Rounding rule (recommended for MSA): 
   "Monthly token usage will be aggregated per account and rounded to the nearest one thousand (1,000) tokens for billing purposes. Rounding is applied after banded token allocation and before discounts or credits."

2) Band-proration example clause: 
   "If a single request/response spans multiple context bands, tokens will be apportioned to the applicable band(s) based on raw token counts and billed at the rates applicable to each band."

3) Pilot concession example (sample clause):
   "For the initial 30-day pilot period, Redwood will apply a smoothing credit equal to 50% of tokens billed at the 32k+ premium band, capped at $5,000. Any credits will be reflected as a line item on the invoice and are non-refundable."

4) Alternative to hard minimum (for procurement preference): offer a waived minimum for duration of pilot but require a commitment to a short-term reserved capacity if usage consistently exceeds X tokens/day.

Ben — can you confirm the math in Naomi's sample CSV and whether our billing system can express the smoothing credit as a discrete invoice line?

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Sr. Account Executive, Redwood Inference

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Invoice sample + billing boundary clarifications

Kimberly — confirming on the mechanics. A couple of implementation notes: 

- The attached calc_breakdown.pdf shows step-by-step math and how our billing pipeline applies banded rates before rounding. Important: rounding to the nearest 1,000 happens on the monthly aggregated sum per band, not per-call, to avoid surprising micro-rounding.
- Pilot credits: we add a separate credit line (negative invoice line) marked "Pilot smoothing credit"; accounting treats that as a contra-charge and it reconciles cleanly.
- Edge case: if a customer's aggregated monthly tokens are below the 10k minimum and they requested a waiver, the waiver produces a zeroed invoice for the month but still logs the usage for true-up.

Sample numbers (from Naomi's CSV):
- Aggregated banded usage: 0-8k: 7,000 tokens; 8k-32k: 85,600 tokens; 32k+: 6,200 tokens.
- Pre-round totals: 98,800 tokens.
- After rounding to nearest 1,000: 99,000 tokens.
- Billing order: apply banded pricing -> compute subtotal -> apply pilot credit (if any) -> compute tax/tiered discounts -> generate invoice.

I can export the calc_breakdown.pdf and the system-ready line items if Jane wants the exact file to attach to the procurement packet.

—Ben
Ben Carter
Billing Lead, Redwood Inference
